memories.memory: The decision was made to keep the API server on Hono due to its middleware model covering authentication, logging, and rate-limiting with minimal overhead. It runs the same on Node and edge runtimes. Express was considered but rejected for having a larger dependency surface and slower cold starts; Fastify was also evaluated but found to provide no measurable gains over Hono for the workload.

The decision for the apps/dashboard/src/store.ts was to use Zustand for client state in the dashboard, as it efficiently covers the small global state surface (session, filters, toasts) in about 50 lines without unnecessary complexity.

The team considered and rejected Redux Toolkit due to excessive boilerplate and indirection, which led to spending more time on slices than on features during the spike. MobX was also rejected because implicit reactivity made it difficult to trace renders during the spike.

The decision for the packages/api/src/db.ts is to query Postgres using the postgres.js driver with hand-written SQL. This approach is favored because direct SQL keeps query plans visible and avoids a runtime abstraction layer, with typed row mappers living next to each query.
Prisma was considered and rejected due to its query engine adding cold-start latency on serverless deployments and hiding generated SQL, which impacted performance during the 2026-02 spike.
TypeORM was also rejected because its decorator-based entities conflicted with the functional style of the codebase.

The decision for packages/api/src/http.ts is to use native fetch with a small retry wrapper for outbound HTTP, as Node 18+ includes fetch natively. The wrapper adds retries, timeouts, and JSON handling without any additional dependency.

The decision to use native fetch was made after considering and rejecting Axios due to interceptor chains obscuring a double-retry bug identified in January 2026, and Request because it is deprecated since 2020 and has unpatched vulnerabilities.

The decision for packages/api/src/auth/session.ts is to store session tokens in httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies. This approach keeps tokens out of reach of injected scripts, as the browser attaches them automatically without the SPA touching the raw token.

The team considered and rejected localStorage for session token storage due to XSS exfiltration risks, highlighted by the 2026-04 pentest which demonstrated token theft through a compromised analytics snippet accessing localStorage. sessionStorage was also rejected for having the same XSS exposure and the additional issue of tokens being lost with every new tab.

The decision for the packages/api/package.json is to run unit tests with the built-in node:test runner due to zero test-framework dependencies. running node --test directly executes TypeScript output and requires no transform config for CI. Jest was rejected due to ongoing ESM support transform workarounds and config drift issues during the 2026-03 attempt. Vitest was also considered but found unnecessary as node:test meets their needs without adding extra dependencies.

The decision for apps/dashboard/tailwind.config.ts was to style the dashboard using Tailwind utility classes, as it avoids runtime style computation, integrates well with React Server Components, and maintains design tokens in one configuration file.

The team rejected styled-components due to its runtime CSS-in-JS incompatibility with React Server Components and an additional ~12KB to the bundle size during the spike. CSS Modules were also considered workable but were not preferred due to styling being split across files.

The decision for packages/api/src/cache.ts is to cache session lookups in a Postgres UNLOGGED table, which benchmarks within 15% of Redis for the session read pattern and keeps the stack at exactly one datastore.

The team rejected Redis for caching due to the operational budget decision to maintain only one datastore until scale requires revisiting at 10x traffic. In-process memory cache was rejected for breaking under multiple API instances, and sticky sessions were also not considered due to deployment constraints.

The decision for packages/api/migrations/README.md is to use hand-written, numbered, forward-only SQL migrations, as every schema change is reviewed as literal SQL to maintain linear production and CI history.

The rationale for forward-only SQL migrations is that auto-generated migrations were rejected due to issues in March 2026 when a generated diff caused a column drop that reached staging, leading to a rollback.

Generated Data Definition Language (DDL) for schema changes is no longer trusted due to previous failures, and down migrations were rejected on the basis of false confidence as most destructive changes cannot be reversed.
The team concluded that the real method of rollback is to restore from backups, rather than relying on down migrations.

The decision was made to keep the public API as REST with an OpenAPI specification, favoring HTTP caching, straightforward authentication, and the availability of mature tooling in every client language. Sparse fieldsets were chosen to address overfetching concerns.

The team considered and rejected GraphQL due to the complexity of resolver N+1s and cache invalidation, which were deemed to outweigh the flexibility for their ~30-endpoint surface during an evaluation in May 2026 with the mobile team present.
The team also evaluated tRPC but decided against it as public consumers are not all TypeScript, which would lock the contract to a single language ecosystem.

The decision for packages/api/src/logger.ts is to use structured logging with pino, generating one JSON line per request for fast and structured logging, as ops dashboards can parse JSON lines natively.

The decision for .github/workflows/ci.yml is that CI runs on GitHub Actions with a single reusable workflow, rationalized by the use of one workflow file with a matrix per package and no CI vendor lock beyond the implications of the repository host.

User's team decided to use pnpm workspace for the monorepo. The rationale includes a strict node_modules layout that catches phantom dependencies and a workspace protocol that keeps internal packages linked.

The decision for packages/api/src/middleware.ts is to implement token-bucket rate limiting at the API edge per API key, as it provides predictable burst behavior with limits configured according to plan tiers.

The decision for packages/api/src/errors.ts is that all API errors will use the problem+json envelope, as per RFC 7807, providing clients with a uniform error shape while mapping internal codes to documented types.
User's team decided that local development runs through Docker Compose, allowing Postgres and the API to start with one command, ensuring parity with the deploy image.

User's team decided to use Prettier with the shared config and ESLint flat config for lint rules in eslint.config.js. The rationale is that formatting is not reviewed while lint rules are, and keeping the tools separate maintains speed.

User's team decided on feature flags to be read from environment variables without a flag service, as a dozen flags do not justify a flag platform; environment variables allow for atomic deployment with the code.

The decision for packages/api/src/telemetry.ts is to export OpenTelemetry traces to the collector, sampled at 10%. The rationale is to utilize vendor-neutral instrumentation while keeping ingest costs flat.

User decided that file uploads for packages/api/src/uploads.ts will go to S3-compatible object storage instead of the database. This decision aims to keep the database small and ensure faster backups, utilizing presigned URLs to offload the file transfer process.
User decided that Zod schemas will validate every API input at the boundary for packages/api/src/schemas.ts. This approach allows one schema per endpoint to serve as the OpenAPI source of truth.

User decided to version the API in the URL path (/v1) for packages/api/openapi.yaml, where breaking changes will increment the version. This approach is considered explicit and cache-friendly, addressing previous confusion experienced by two integration partners with header versioning.

User's team decided that each package in the monorepo will have its own README file containing run and test instructions. This decision is rationalized by placing the onboarding documentation next to the code it describes.

User's team decided that UI strings will go through the i18n catalog from the start, based on the rationale that retrofitting i18n was a six-week project at their last company and implementing a catalog-first approach is cost-effective now.

reply.proposal: Refactor the HTTP middleware stack in packages/api/src/middleware.ts to use Hono's built-in middleware composition model with explicit ordering: authentication → rate limiting → request logging → response handling. Extract each concern into a separate, testable middleware function that follows Hono's standard signature, then compose them in a single middleware chain at the router level. - The team considered and rejected localStorage for session token storage due to XSS exfiltration risks, highlighted by the 2026-04 pentest which demonstrated token theft through a compromised analytics snippet accessing localStorage. sessionStorage was also rejected for having the same XSS exposure and the additional issue of tokens being lost with every new tab.

- The decision for packages/api/src/logger.ts is to use structured logging with pino, generating one JSON line per request for fast and structured logging, as ops dashboards can parse JSON lines natively.

reply.proposal: Maintain httpOnly cookies for secure storage while adding a separate, non-sensitive session metadata cookie (e.g., `sessionId` or `isAuthenticated`) that the SPA can read to determine auth state. For fetch calls, continue relying on the browser's automatic cookie attachment via credentials: 'include' rather than having JavaScript manually read and attach tokens. If the SPA genuinely needs to know the token value for application logic (not just sending it), this indicates a design issue—the token should remain opaque to the client, and any needed claims should be exposed via a separate `/me` endpoint that returns user metadata. This preserves the XSS protection from our prior pentest learnings while giving the SPA the auth awareness it needs.
acknowledged_rejections: localStorage or sessionStorage for token storage—rejected in prior pentest due to XSS exfiltration risks demonstrated via compromised analytics snippet
Making the session token itself readable from JavaScript—contradicts the security decision to keep tokens out of reach of injected scripts

reply.proposal: Extend the existing Tailwind utility class approach to the marketing pages, maintaining consistency with the dashboard styling strategy. Create a shared component library within apps/dashboard that colocates Tailwind classes with component logic through well-organized component files and a centralized tailwind.config.ts that defines all design tokens. This preserves the runtime efficiency and RSC compatibility we've already validated, avoids bundle bloat, and allows component-scoped styling through logical file organization (e.g., components/marketing/Hero/Hero.tsx with all its Tailwind classes) rather than separate style files. CSS Modules (rejected: styling split across files conflicts with component colocation preference)
CSS-in-JS solutions (rejected: prior team decision against runtime style computation)

In-process memory cache was rejected for breaking under multiple API instances, and sticky sessions were also not considered due to deployment constraints.

reply.proposal: Implement a query-result cache in the existing Postgres UNLOGGED table by adding a materialized session view with a short TTL (e.g., 30-60 seconds) that stores the most recent session validation state, indexed by session token hash. This leverages our already-approved single-datastore constraint and the benchmarked performance of Postgres for session reads. Add an in-memory LRU cache (e.g., node-lru-cache) within each API instance with a 5-10 second TTL to absorb repeated lookups within a single request lifecycle or rapid consecutive requests, falling back to the Postgres view on miss. This two-tier approach avoids the multi-instance coherency problems that rejected pure in-process caching while staying within our operational budget of one datastore.
key_technologies: Postgres materialized view or trigger-based refresh
acknowledged_rejections: Redis caching—rejected due to operational budget constraint to maintain single datastore until 10x traffic
Pure in-process memory cache—rejected because it breaks coherency across multiple API instances
Sticky sessions—rejected due to deployment constraints
